Subject: RFI: burst behavior + tail decomposition questions

Hi Grace,

Thanks again for the quick onboarding call yesterday. As we finalize our RFI packet for the inference platform evaluation, we have a couple of technical clarifications around stability during burst events and how you decompose tail latency. These items are blockers for our procurement team. Could you provide short-form answers to the two bullets below and any empirical evidence you can share (workbook, plots, configs)?

1) Burst tolerance: describe the test we should expect Redwood to run to simulate a 10-20x short-term burst (duration 30s-5m) on a reserved pool. Include the traffic shaping approach, concurrency profile, and what metrics you capture to determine 'no-service-impact'.

2) Tail decomposition: how do you attribute 95th/99th percentile latency to factors like KV-cache misses, model-side compute variation, scheduler queuing, and cold-replica spin-up? What counters/metrics and instrumentation do you expose to customers?

We'd like any example artifacts you can attach (charts, run configs, a short summary spreadsheet). Procurement prefers concise answers they can paste into the RFI.

Appreciate it — please loop in anyone on your side who should respond in detail.

Best,
Alex

From: grace_oconnor@redwood.com

Alex — thanks for the clear ask. Looping in Marissa (solutions) and Dev (infra/benchmarks) for the detailed artifacts. Below is a concise response for procurement; Dev and I will follow up with the workbook and run configs this afternoon.

Quick answers (procurement-friendly):

1) Burst tolerance: We run a controlled burst test that ramps steady-state QPS to a target burst multiplier (10x or 20x) using a closed-loop driver over three stages: ramp (10–30s), sustain (30s–5m), and drain (30s). Traffic mix mirrors production: mean tokens per request, streaming vs non-streaming ratio, and an embedding-only control. Key pass/fail criteria: no 5xx error rate increase above baseline + <10% throughput degradation for other tenants (for shared pools) or <5% latency uplift for dedicated pools. We capture per-replica QPS, inflight requests, scheduler queue length, KV cache hit rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, and GPU utilization.

2) Tail decomposition: We instrument at hop boundaries and attribute percentile slices using a waterfall tracing approach. Primary attribution buckets: KV-cache miss time (lookup + KV fill), model decode time variance (per-step GPU kernels), host-side queuing (scheduler wait + batching delay), and cold-replica startup time. Customers get time-series for each bucket and per-request taggable traces for sampling.

Attachments we'll send: a short workbook with representative burst runs, a one-page methodology PDF, and the exact run-configs used.

Next steps: Dev will attach the artifacts. If procurement wants, we can produce a 2-page executive summary version specifically styled for the RFI.

Thanks,
Grace
Grace O'Connor
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Grace — that summary looks good. A couple of short follow-ups that procurement wants captured explicitly in the RFI table: 

- During the burst sustain phase, do you rely on autoscale (spin up new replicas) or do you accept throughput degradation on existing replicas? If autoscale, what is typical spin-up time per replica and do you have metrics on the percentage of requests routed to new replicas during spin-up?

- For KV-cache misses, are those served from a local LRU on-host cache or a shared remote cache? If on-host, how do you handle cache warming for canary traffic?

If you can add numeric examples (e.g., spin-up ~45s for GPU cold start, cache warm-up <3s for small prefix sets) that will be helpful.

From: dev_patel@redwood.com
To: Alex Moreno <alex.moreno@dataworks.com>, grace_oconnor@redwood.com
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: 2027-09-03T14:47:00-07:00
Subject: Re: RFI: burst behavior + tail decomposition questions

Alex — hi, Dev from infra here. Per Grace's note, attaching the detailed workbook and methodology. Below are explicit numeric answers and a short methodology snippet you can paste into the RFI table.

Numeric examples (representative from a 16-GPU dedicated pool running a 7B decoder model, token length distribution matching your sample workload):
- Burst handling: Our policy is hybrid: aggressive batching + autoscale. During the first 30–60s of a large burst we prioritize latency SLOs using adaptive batching (reduces per-token latency impact); if sustained beyond configured sustain timeout (default 60s for Dedicated), autoscaler begins adding replicas. Typical new replica readiness (container + model load into GPU memory using our cold-load fast-path) is ~35–75s depending on model size and quantization. Measured median spin-up in our lab for similar configs: 48s.

- Impact routing: While new replicas come online we route traffic using progressive cutover: initially 80/20 split to warm replicas vs new replicas and move to 50/50 after health checks. During spin-up we observe ~12–22% of sustained requests hitting new replicas (varies by ramp aggressiveness).

KV-cache behavior:
- Cache architecture: per-host LRU prefix cache with optional shared warm-cache layer for high-churn workloads. Default Dedicated installs are on-host LRU for lowest lookup latency.
- Warm-up and canaries: For canaries we pre-warm cache by replaying representative prefixes (from stored seed sets) to the canary before traffic cutover; warm-up for a small prefix set (<=5k prefixes) is typically <3s to reach 80% hit rate for the working set.

Instrumentation and signals exposed to customers (what you'll see in the RFI):
- Per-request sampled trace with timestamps for: ingress, scheduler_enqueue, batch_start, batch_end, kv_lookup_start, kv_lookup_end, model_start, model_end, egress.
- Aggregated timeseries: kv_hit_rate, per-replica queue_len, batch_size_distribution, p50/p90/p95/p99 for decode-only and end-to-end, gpu_utilization, container_start_time, model_load_time.

Attached artifacts (zipped in the Drive link):
- redwood_stability_methodology.pdf — one-page methodology + metric definitions.
- redwood_burst_analysis_v1.xlsx — workbook: sample run spreadsheets, charts (p95/p99 vs time), heatmaps for queue length.
- run-configs.yaml — exact load-driver config we used in the runs.

Paste-ready snippet for your RFI table:
"""
Burst tolerance: Redwood runs staged bursts (ramp 10–30s, sustain 30s–5m, drain 30s) using production-like request mixes. Hybrid handling: adaptive batching to preserve latency SLOs + autoscale after sustain timeout (default 60s). Replica spin-up median ~48s (range 35–75s); traffic progressively shifts to new replicas (initial ~20% to new replicas). KV-cache: per-host LRU by default with optional shared warm-cache; small prefix warm-up to 80% hit rate typically <3s. Exposed metrics: per-request traces (kv/model/batch timestamps), kv_hit_rate, per-replica queue_len, batch_size_distribution, p50/p95/p99.
"""

If there are specific numbers you need for other model classes (13B/70B) or for burst magnitudes beyond 20x, we can generate a short appendix — that takes a couple of hours of runs. The Drive link above has the artifacts and a short slide for your procurement pack.

Cheers,
Dev Patel
Infra Lead, Redwood Inference
